title: VI. The First Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: This was the third time Ivan had gone to see Smerdyakov since coming back from Moscow. The first time he'd seen and talked with him was on the day he arrived; then he'd visited once more, two weeks later. But his visits had stopped after that second one, so that it had now been over a month since he'd seen him. And he'd heard almost nothing about him since.

Ivan hadn't returned until five days after his father's death, so he wasn't there for the funeral, which took place the day before he got back. The reason for the delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his Moscow address, had had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph him, and she, not knowing his address either, had telegraphed his sister and aunt, counting on Ivan visiting them as soon as he arrived in Moscow. But he didn't go to see them until four days after he got there. When he received the telegram, he had, of course, set off for our town at once. Alyosha was the first to meet him, and Ivan was quite surprised to find that, against the general opinion in town, Alyosha refused to suspect Mitya at all, and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later, after seeing the police captain and the prosecutor, and hearing the details of the charge and arrest, he was even more surprised at Alyosha, and put his opinion down only to an exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond of.

Let's say a word or two here about Ivan's feelings toward his brother Dmitri. He genuinely disliked him; at most he sometimes felt a kind of pity for him, and even that was mixed with a great deal of contempt, nearly revulsion. Mitya's whole personality, even his appearance, was deeply unappealing to him. Ivan looked with indignation on Katerina Ivanovna's love for his brother. And yet he went to see Mitya on the very first day he arrived, and that meeting, far from shaking Ivan's belief in his guilt, actually strengthened it. He found his brother agitated, nervously worked up. Mitya had been talkative, but scattered and incoherent. He'd used violent language, accused Smerdyakov, and been terribly confused. He'd talked mostly about the three thousand roubles, which he said had been "stolen" from him by his father.
"The money was mine, it was my money," Mitya kept repeating. "Even if I had stolen it, I'd have had the right to."

He barely disputed the evidence against him, and when he did try to turn some fact in his favor, it was in an absurd, incoherent way. He seemed to have hardly any wish to defend himself, to Ivan or to anyone else. Quite the opposite—he was angry, and proudly contemptuous of the charges against him; he kept flaring up and abusing everyone. He only laughed scornfully at Grigory's testimony about the open door, and declared it was "the devil who opened it." But he couldn't offer any coherent explanation for the fact. He even managed to insult Ivan during their first meeting, telling him sharply that people who declared "everything is permitted" had no business suspecting and questioning him. On the whole he was anything but friendly toward Ivan that day. Right after that meeting with Mitya, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov for the first time.

On the train from Moscow, he'd kept thinking about Smerdyakov and about their last conversation, on the evening before Ivan left. A number of things struck him as puzzling and suspicious. But when he gave his testimony to the investigating lawyer, Ivan said nothing, for the time being, about that conversation. He put it off until he'd seen Smerdyakov, who was in the hospital at the time.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, confidently assured Ivan, in answer to his persistent questions, that Smerdyakov's epileptic attack was unmistakably genuine, and seemed genuinely surprised that Ivan would ask whether he might have faked it on the day of the murder. They gave him to understand that the attack had been an exceptional one, the fits recurring several times, so that the patient's life had actually been in danger, and it was only now, after treatment, that they could say with confidence he would survive. "Though it's quite possible," added Doctor Herzenstube, "that his reason will be impaired for a good while, if not permanently." When Ivan asked impatiently whether that meant he was now insane, they told him that wasn't the case yet, not in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities were noticeable. Ivan decided to find out for himself what those abnormalities were.

At the hospital he was allowed to see the patient right away. Smerdyakov was lying on a narrow bed in a separate ward. There was only one other bed in the room, occupied by a tradesman from town, swollen with dropsy, who was clearly close to death; he'd be no obstacle to their conversation. Smerdyakov gave an uncertain grin on seeing Ivan, and for the first instant seemed nervous—or so Ivan imagined, at least. But that passed quickly. For the rest of the visit, Ivan was struck, instead, by Smerdyakov's composure. From the first glance Ivan had no doubt he was very ill. He was very weak; he spoke slowly, as if his tongue moved with difficulty; he'd grown much thinner and more sallow. Throughout the visit, which lasted twenty minutes, he kept complaining of headache and aching in all his limbs. His thin, sexless face seemed to have shrunk; his hair was disheveled, and the tuft of curls at his forehead stood up in a thin clump. But in the left eye, screwed up as if hinting at something, Smerdyakov remained unchanged. "It's always worth talking to a clever man"—Ivan was reminded of that at once. He sat down on the stool at the foot of the bed. Smerdyakov, with visible effort, shifted his position, but he wasn't the one to speak first. He stayed silent, and didn't even seem especially interested.
"Can you talk to me?" Ivan asked. "I won't tire you out."
"Certainly I can," Smerdyakov mumbled, in a faint voice. "Has your honor been back long?" he added, in a condescending tone, as if reassuring a nervous visitor.
"I only arrived today.... To see the mess you've gotten yourself into here."
Smerdyakov sighed.
"Why are you sighing? You knew about it the whole time," Ivan blurted out.
Smerdyakov stayed stolidly silent for a while.
"How could I not know? It was obvious beforehand. But how could I have known it would turn out like this?"
"What would turn out like what? Don't dodge! You predicted you'd have a fit—on the way down to the cellar, you know. You named the very spot."
"Have you already said that at the inquiry?" Smerdyakov asked calmly.
Ivan suddenly felt a surge of anger.
"No, not yet, but I certainly will. You'll have to explain a great deal to me, my man, and let me tell you, I'm not going to let you play games with me!"
"Why would I play games with you, when I trust you completely, the way I trust God Almighty?" Smerdyakov said, with the same composure, only closing his eyes for a moment.

"In the first place," Ivan began, "I know epileptic fits can't be predicted in advance. I've asked around—don't try to fool me. You can't foretell the day and hour. So how did you tell me the day and the hour in advance, and about the cellar too? How could you know you'd fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, unless you faked the fit on purpose?"

"I had to go down to the cellar anyway, several times a day, in fact," Smerdyakov drawled out slowly. "I fell from the loft the same way a year ago. It's quite true you can't predict the exact day and hour of a fit, but you can always sense one coming."
"But you did predict the day and the hour!"
"When it comes to my epilepsy, sir, you'd do much better to ask the doctors here about it. You can ask them whether it was a real fit or a fake one. There's no use my saying anything more about it."
"And the cellar? How could you know about the cellar in advance?"

"You just can't seem to get past that cellar! As I was going down, I was in a state of terrible dread and doubt. What frightened me most was the thought of losing you and being left with no protection in the whole world. So I went down into the cellar thinking, 'Here it comes, it'll strike me down any second, will I fall?' And it was exactly that fear that brought on the spasm that always comes over me... and down I went. All of that, and everything I'd told you at the gate the evening before—how frightened I was, and what I said about the cellar—I told all of it to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it's all been written down in the record. And Dr. Varvinsky here insisted to all of them that it was precisely the thought of it, the fear that I might fall, that brought it on. That's exactly when the fit seized me. So they wrote it down that this is just how it must have happened, simply from my fear."
As he finished, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as if worn out.

"So you've said all that in your testimony?" Ivan asked, somewhat caught off guard. He'd meant to frighten him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and it turned out Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.
"What would I have to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth," Smerdyakov said firmly.
"And did you tell them every word of our conversation at the gate?"
"No, not every word, I wouldn't say."
"And did you tell them you could fake fits, the way you bragged to me then?"
"No, I didn't tell them that either."
"Tell me now—why did you send me to Tchermashnya, then?"
"I was afraid you'd go off to Moscow; Tchermashnya's closer, anyway."
"You're lying; you suggested my leaving on your own; you told me to get out of the way of trouble."

"That was simply out of affection and genuine devotion to you—foreseeing trouble in the house, I wanted to spare you it. Only I wanted to spare myself even more. That's why I told you to get out of harm's way—so that you'd understand there was going to be trouble in the house, and would stay home to protect your father."
"You could have said it more directly, you blockhead!" Ivan suddenly flared up.

"How could I have said it more directly, at the time? It was pure fear that made me speak at all, and you might have gotten angry too. I might well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and carry off that money, since he considered it his own; but who could have guessed it would end in a murder like this? I thought he'd only carry off the three thousand lying under the master's mattress in the envelope, and instead, you see, he's murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?"
"But if you're telling me yourself it couldn't be guessed, how could I have guessed and stayed home? You're contradicting yourself!" Ivan said, thinking it over.
"You might have guessed it from the fact that I sent you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow."
"How could I have guessed anything from that?"
Smerdyakov seemed quite worn out, and fell silent again for a minute.

"You might have guessed it from my asking you not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya—because I wanted you nearer, since Moscow's a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you weren't far away, wouldn't have dared to be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come to protect me too, since I warned you about Grigory Vassilyevitch being ill, and that I was afraid I'd have a fit. And when I explained those knocks to you, the ones you could use to get in to see the deceased, and how Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you'd realize for yourself that he was sure to do something, and so you wouldn't even go to Tchermashnya, but would stay."
"He talks very coherently," Ivan thought, "even if he does mumble. What's this derangement of his faculties Herzenstube was talking about?"
"You're being sly with me, damn you!" he exclaimed, growing angry.
"But I thought at the time that you'd guessed everything," Smerdyakov parried, with the most innocent air.
"If I'd guessed, I would have stayed," Ivan cried.
"Well, I thought it was exactly because you'd guessed that you left in such a hurry—just to get away from trouble, just to run and save yourself in your fright."
"You think everyone's as much a coward as you are?"
"Forgive me, I thought you were like me."

"Of course, I ought to have guessed," Ivan said, agitated; "and I did guess there was some mischief brewing on your part... only you're lying, you're lying again," he cried, suddenly remembering. "Do you recall going up to the carriage and saying to me, 'It's always worth talking to a clever man'? So you were glad I was leaving, since you praised me for it?"
Smerdyakov sighed, again and again. A trace of color crept into his face.

"If I was pleased," he said, rather breathlessly, "it was simply because you agreed not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya. Because it was closer, anyway. Only when I said those words to you, it wasn't meant as praise—it was a reproach. You didn't understand it that way."
"What reproach?"
"Why, that foreseeing such a disaster, you abandoned your own father, and wouldn't protect us—because I could have been arrested any moment for stealing that three thousand."
"Damn you!" Ivan swore again. "Wait—did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?"
"I told them everything exactly as it was."
Ivan found himself puzzled again.

"If I thought of anything back then," he began again, "it was only some piece of mischief on your part. That Dmitri might kill him, yes—but that he would steal, I didn't believe that at the time.... But I was prepared for any kind of mischief from you. You told me yourself you could fake a fit. Why did you say that?"

"That was pure simplemindedness, and I've never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it then to show off to you. It was just foolishness. I liked you so much back then, and was open with you."
"My brother accuses you outright of the murder and the theft."

"What else is left for him to do?" Smerdyakov said, with a bitter grin. "And who's going to believe him, with all the evidence stacked against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say after that? But never mind him! He's trembling just to save his own skin."
He fell slowly silent; then suddenly, as if on second thought, he added:

"And look at this too. He wants to pin it on me, make it out that it's my doing—I've already heard that. But as for me being clever enough to fake a fit—would I have told you beforehand that I could fake one, if I'd really had such a scheme against your father in mind? If I'd been planning a murder like that, could I have been fool enough to give evidence like that against myself in advance? And to his son, no less! I ask you! Is that likely? As if such a thing could happen—nothing like it ever has. No one's hearing this conversation of ours now except Providence itself, and if you told the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch about it, you could clear me completely just by doing so, because who would be such a criminal, if he's so open about it in advance? Anyone can see that."

"Well," and Ivan got up to cut the conversation short, struck by Smerdyakov's last argument. "I don't suspect you at all, and I think it's absurd, really, to suspect you. On the contrary, I'm grateful to you for setting my mind at ease. Now I'll go, but I'll come again. In the meantime, good-bye. Get well. Is there anything you need?"
"I'm very thankful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn't forget me, and provides whatever I need, out of her kindness. Good people visit me every day."
"Good-bye. But I won't say anything about your being able to fake a fit, and I don't advise you to either," something made Ivan say suddenly.
"I understand completely. And if you don't speak of that, I won't say anything about our conversation at the gate."

With that, Ivan went out, and only after he'd gone a dozen steps down the corridor did he suddenly feel that there'd been an insulting undertone in Smerdyakov's last words. He very nearly turned back, but it was only a passing impulse, and muttering "Nonsense!" he walked out of the hospital.

His main feeling was one of relief at the thought that it wasn't Smerdyakov, but Mitya, who'd committed the murder—though one might have expected the opposite. He didn't want to examine the reason for this feeling, and even felt a genuine reluctance to pry into his own sensations. He felt as if he wanted to hurry up and forget something. In the days that followed, he became convinced of Mitya's guilt, as he learned the full weight of the evidence against him. There was testimony from people of no particular importance, Fenya and her mother, for instance, but its effect was nearly overwhelming. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern, and at Plotnikov's shop, as well as the witnesses at Mokroe, their testimony seemed conclusive. It was the details that were so damning. The secret of the knocks struck the lawyers almost as forcefully as Grigory's testimony about the open door. Grigory's wife, Marfa, in answer to Ivan's questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain the whole night on the other side of the partition wall. "He wasn't three paces from our bed," and that although she was a sound sleeper, she'd woken several times and heard him moaning—"He was moaning the whole time, moaning without stopping."
Talking with Herzenstube, and offering his opinion that Smerdyakov wasn't insane, just rather weak, Ivan got only a subtle smile out of the old man in response.

"Do you know how he spends his time now?" he asked. "Memorizing lists of French words. He's got a notebook under his pillow with the French words written out for him in Russian letters by somebody, heh heh heh!"

Ivan eventually dismissed all his doubts. He couldn't think of Dmitri without revulsion. One thing was strange, though. Alyosha kept insisting that Dmitri wasn't the murderer, and that "in all likelihood" it was Smerdyakov. Ivan always felt that Alyosha's opinion meant a great deal to him, and so he was startled by it now. Another odd thing was that Alyosha made no attempt to talk about Mitya with Ivan—never brought the subject up himself, and only answered when asked. This, too, struck Ivan as particularly strange.

But he was very preoccupied at the time with something quite separate from all this. On returning from Moscow, he'd given himself over hopelessly to his mad, consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This isn't the place to begin describing this new passion of Ivan's, one that left its mark on the rest of his life: it would furnish material for a whole other novel, one I may never write. But I can't leave out the fact that when Ivan, on leaving Katerina Ivanovna's with Alyosha, as I've already told, said to him, "I'm not especially keen on her," it was an outright lie: he loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much he could have killed her. Many things had combined to produce this feeling in him. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she had rushed to meet Ivan on his return as her one salvation. She'd been hurt, insulted, humiliated in her feelings. And here was the man who'd come back to her, the one who had once loved her so ardently before (oh, she knew that very well), and whose heart and mind she considered so far above her own. But this sternly virtuous woman didn't give herself over entirely to the man she loved, despite the Karamazov violence of his passions and the powerful hold he had on her. She was tormented, at the same time, by constant remorse for having abandoned Mitya, and in moments of conflict and violent anger (and there were many of them), she told Ivan so, plainly. This was what he'd called to Alyosha "lie upon lie." There was, of course, plenty that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything else.... But more on this later.

For a time he did, in fact, nearly forget Smerdyakov existed, and yet, two weeks after his first visit to him, he began to be haunted by the same strange thoughts as before. Suffice it to say that he kept asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, he'd crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened to hear what his father was doing below. Why had he recalled that afterward with revulsion? Why, the next morning, had he suddenly grown so depressed on his journey? Why, on reaching Moscow, had he said to himself, "I am a scoundrel"? And now he almost fancied these tormenting thoughts might make him forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so completely did they take hold of him again. It was right after this thought occurred to him that he ran into Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and put a question to him:

"Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterward, out in the yard, I told you I reserved 'the right to desire'?... Tell me, did you think, at the time, that I wanted father dead, or not?"
"I did think so," Alyosha answered softly.

"It was true, too; it wasn't just guesswork. But didn't you also imagine, back then, that what I actually wanted was for 'one reptile to devour another'—that is, exactly for Dmitri to kill father, and as soon as possible... and that I myself was even prepared to help make that happen?"
Alyosha went rather pale, and looked silently into his brother's face.
"Speak!" Ivan cried. "I want more than anything to know what you thought at the time. I want the truth, the truth!"
He drew a deep breath, looking angrily at Alyosha before the answer came.
"Forgive me, I did think that too, at the time," Alyosha whispered, and added no softening word to it.

"Thanks," Ivan snapped, and, leaving Alyosha, walked quickly away. From that time on, Alyosha noticed that Ivan began plainly avoiding him, and seemed even to have taken a dislike to him—so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. Right after that meeting, Ivan hadn't gone home, but had gone straight back to Smerdyakov.
